result:
The proposed answer, N(N−1)/2, is most likely wrong, and I could not derive the correct count here.

The weakest point is the N=1 case. The algebraic soliton is a regular solution on the real line. Its tau function is real-valued on the real axis and has no real zeros, so its zeros come in complex-conjugate pairs. Degree 2 in x then gives one pole in the upper half-plane. The proposed solution instead claims the N=1 pole sits on the real axis and gives 0 poles in the upper half-plane. That contradicts regularity.

The "one pole per pair of solitons" argument is also unsupported. It is not derived from the double-Wronskian structure. The degree claim ("N zeros approach the real line") conflicts with the fact that the real solutions have no real poles.

A more natural count is that the tau function has about 2N² zeros, split evenly by conjugation. That gives N² poles in the upper half-plane, which matches N=1. I am recalling this from the literature rather than deriving it, so I am not certain of N². Either way, the proposed formula fails the N=1 check.

VERDICT: REJECT
